stories.title: Those Bumpy Yellow Tiles Are Causing Trouble
stories.headline_kid: The bumpy tactile tiles that help blind people walk safely are tripping up wheelchairs, prams and even grown-ups!
summary: You have probably felt those bumpy yellow or grey tiles near pedestrian crossings and void decks in your HDB estate. They are called tactile tiles, and they help people who cannot see well to feel the path with their feet or walking cane, so they know when a crossing or staircase is near.

The problem is that some residents say these tiles become slippery when wet, especially after rain. Wheelchair wheels and pram wheels can also get stuck in the bumps, and some elderly people have slipped and fallen while walking over them.

The Land Transport Authority is already planning to swap out the tiles at pedestrian crossings for a safer new design. Now, some residents want Housing Board estates to get the same careful review, so walkways near homes are safer for everyone too.

This shows something tricky: a feature built to help one group of people (the visually impaired) can accidentally create a new problem for another group (the elderly or people with wheels). Singapore is now trying to find a design that keeps everyone safe.

lenses.me: Next time you cycle or scoot near your void deck, look out for tactile tiles, especially when the floor is wet.
lenses.family: If your grandparents use a walking stick or wheelchair, remind them to be extra careful crossing these tiled areas.
lenses.friends: Your friends who ride bicycles or push scooters around the estate might notice their wheels wobble over the bumps too.
lenses.nation: Singapore is redesigning public spaces so they work well for blind residents, elderly folks and everyone in between.
lenses.world: Many cities around the world face this same challenge: how to build one thing that keeps every kind of person safe.

stories.title: Do Fancy University Rankings Really Tell the Whole Story?
stories.headline_kid: Asian universities are climbing up the world rankings, but does that change what people think is a 'good' university?
summary: Every year, groups like QS publish lists ranking the world's best universities. Lately, universities in Asia — including in Singapore, China and Hong Kong — have been climbing higher and higher on these lists.

But a writer points out that just because a university's rank goes up on paper, people's opinions about which schools are 'prestigious' or impressive do not always change so fast. Many families still dream of famous universities in places like the UK or the US, even if an Asian university now ranks just as high.

This matters because choosing a university is a big decision that affects your whole future — the courses you take, the friends you make, and even the job opportunities you get later. Rankings are useful, but they are not the only thing that makes a university a good fit for a person.

For Singapore, this is a proud moment because our own universities like NUS and NTU are regularly ranked among the best in the world. It shows that hard work and good teaching can build a strong reputation, even without hundreds of years of history.

lenses.me: One day you will choose where to study — this story reminds us that a school's fame is not the only thing that matters.
lenses.family: Your parents might discuss whether to send you overseas or keep you studying in Singapore when you are older.
lenses.friends: Your friends might talk about 'top' schools — but the best choice is really the one that fits you best.
lenses.nation: Singapore's universities being highly ranked boosts our country's reputation for good education.
lenses.world: This shows how the world's idea of 'the best' education is shifting as Asian countries invest more in their universities.

stories.title: Big Quake in Indonesia Leaves Thousands Without Homes
stories.headline_kid: A massive earthquake shook eastern Indonesia over the weekend, and the number of people who died has now risen to 53.
summary: A huge magnitude-7.7 earthquake struck near Flores island in eastern Indonesia. That is strong enough to badly shake buildings and cause landslides. Sadly, at least 53 people have died, and more than 130 people were injured, many with broken bones.

Around 5,000 people have had to leave their homes and are now staying in shelters. Nearly 160 houses were damaged, along with schools and hospitals. Roads were blocked by landslides, making it harder for rescuers to reach some areas.

Making things worse, aftershocks — smaller earthquakes that follow the big one — kept shaking the ground, slowing down rescue efforts. Thousands of soldiers and police officers have been sent to the region to help search for survivors and clear the roads.

Indonesia sits on something scientists call the 'Ring of Fire', a zone around the Pacific Ocean where earthquakes and volcanoes happen often, because giant pieces of the earth's crust rub against each other there. Since Indonesia is Singapore's close neighbour, many Singaporean families have relatives or holiday plans there, so news like this is followed closely at home.

lenses.me: Imagine the ground suddenly shaking under your feet — that is what earthquake survivors experienced, and it helps to understand why disaster drills matter.
lenses.family: If your family is planning a trip to Indonesia, this is a reminder to check safety updates before travelling.
lenses.friends: You could talk with friends about how Singapore's fire and emergency drills help us stay prepared, even though we rarely get earthquakes.
lenses.nation: Singapore often sends help, like rescue teams or supplies, to support neighbouring countries after big disasters.
lenses.world: This earthquake reminds the world how powerful nature can be, and why countries help each other during emergencies.

stories.title: China Remembers Two Leaders Who Shaped Its Rise
stories.headline_kid: A former Chinese leader named Zhu Rongji has passed away, just days before China honours another leader, Jiang Zemin, on his 100th birthday.
summary: Zhu Rongji, who used to be China's premier (a bit like a prime minister), passed away at the age of 97. He was known for leading huge economic changes in China during the 1990s that helped the country grow richer and stronger.

His death happened just five days before the 100th birth anniversary of Jiang Zemin, who was China's president during that same busy period of change. Together, these two leaders helped open China up to trade and business with the rest of the world.

Because their time in charge overlaps, China is now carefully honouring both men's legacies at once, celebrating what they achieved for the country's growth. Analysts say this is a delicate balancing act for China's current leaders.

Singapore has a special connection here too. Singapore's founding leaders, including Mr Lee Kuan Yew, built close relationships with Chinese leaders like Jiang Zemin over many visits and meetings. Singapore recently mourned Jiang Zemin's passing, showing how these old friendships still matter today, especially since China is one of Singapore's biggest trading partners.

lenses.me: Learning about these leaders helps you understand how big decisions made long ago still affect the world you live in today.
lenses.family: Your family might remember hearing about Singapore's ties with China's leaders through the news or history lessons.
lenses.friends: You could discuss with friends why some countries hold big memorials for their past leaders.
lenses.nation: Singapore's friendly relationship with China's leaders over the decades has helped grow trade and cooperation between the two countries.
lenses.world: China's huge economy affects the whole world, from the toys we buy to the phones we use, so understanding its history helps us understand today's world.

stories.title: The Great Matcha Race: Japan vs China
stories.headline_kid: Everyone from New York to Singapore loves matcha green tea treats — and now Japan and China are racing to grow enough of it!
summary: Matcha is a bright green powdered tea from Japan, used in traditional tea ceremonies for centuries. Lately, it has become super popular around the world — in lattes, ice cream, cakes, and even bubble tea, from cafes in London all the way to Singapore's own malls.

This sudden matcha craze has been great for Japan's tea farmers, bringing new life to an old tradition. But there is a problem: Japan does not have enough farmland to grow all the tea leaves the world now wants, so there is often not enough matcha to go around.

China, which is already the world's biggest tea grower, sees a big opportunity here. It is trying to grow matcha on a much larger scale, which could challenge Japan's long history as the top matcha-maker in the world.

This 'tea rivalry' matters even for us in Singapore. Many kids and families enjoy matcha soft-serve, drinks or desserts at local cafes. If matcha becomes scarcer or more expensive because of high demand worldwide, we might notice higher prices for our favourite matcha treats too.

lenses.me: The next time you eat matcha ice cream, think about the long journey the tea leaves made from a farm in Japan or China to your bowl.
lenses.family: Your family might notice matcha drinks and desserts becoming pricier at cafes if the shortage continues.
lenses.friends: Friends who love matcha bubble tea might be interested to know why it's suddenly everywhere.
lenses.nation: Singapore imports most of its food and drink ingredients, so global food trends like this can affect our cafe menus and prices.
lenses.world: This shows how a craving in one part of the world (like America wanting matcha lattes) can affect farmers and industries far away in Asia.
